title: Justice Leonen concurs with dismissal but says SC should have ruled on Duterte arrest
summary: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen concurred with the Supreme Court's decision to dismiss the consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest in March 2025 on a warrant from the…

blocks.text: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen concurred with the Supreme Court's decision to dismiss the consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest in March 2025 on a warrant from the International Criminal Court but stressed that the court should have also ruled its legality

In his 58-page concurring and dissenting opinion, Leonen agreed to dismiss the petitions for mootness, yet dissented from the majority's failure to “address unresolved, grave, and serious constitutional questions that can recur yet may evade judicial review.”

“I concur in the finding that the Petition for Habeas Corpus should be dismissed. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has competence to determine its own jurisdiction, which includes the disposition of any person physically surrendered to it,” Leonen said.

“However, I dissent from the Court's failure to provide clear guidance for future cases. The situation involves clear, serious, and grave constitutional issues that are capable of repetition and would otherwise evade review. Our silence can be interpreted as complicity in a violation of the Constitution, our concurrence with a treaty, and the relevant law,” he added.
Leonen said that by leaving these questions unanswered, the high court failed to provide much-needed guidelines for future cases.

“The constitutional issues raised in the present Petitions are grave and serious and capable of repetition, yet evading review. This case cannot simply be dismissed on the ground of mootness, even if doing so may be the politically expedient resolution,” Leonen said.

“As the Court of last resort, we must not shirk our duty of providing the clearest guidelines, for the bench and the bar and, by implication, our law enforcement agencies. That is the resolution that would best safeguard and operationalize the human rights provisions under the Rome Statute, which are read through our Constitution,” he added.

Pointing to the risk of similar incidents happening again, Leonen said that Duterte’s purported co-perpetrators remain at large in Philippine territory and “may, at any time, be seized by Philippine authorities and surrendered in the same manner” as the former president.
“In the present case, the manner in which petitioner was seized and surrendered, if repeated in a future case, would evade judicial review,” Leonen said.
The former President was arrested on March 25, 2025 and taken to the Scheveningen prison in The Hague on a warrant of arrest from the ICC.

Duterte is facing charges of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder in connection with the deaths under his war on drugs when he was president of the Philippines and mayor of Davao City.

In separate petitions filed in March 2025, Duterte's youngest daughter Kitty and her half-brothers Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte and Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte asked the SC to order the government to present the former President before the High Court.
The Duterte camp said that the ICC arrest warrant cannot be used as the basis for the arrest and detention of the former president, claiming that it has no jurisdiction in the Philippines.
It said that the ICC may only exercise its jurisdiction if the country’s legal system is not functioning, stressing that the Philippine judicial system is working.
The Philippines withdrew from the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, in 2019 after the Hague-based tribunal began a probe into the Duterte administration's drug war.
Kitty will appeal the decision of the SC.
Duterte's trial before the ICC will start on Nov. 30, 2026.
'Violated rights, equal protection'
Leonen criticized the failure to subject the ICC arrest warrant to Philippine judicial review.

He noted that Duterte should have been promptly brought before a national court—where his identity, the regularity of the arrest, and the observance of his constitutional rights could be confirmed—before any surrender abroad.
Leonen added that the same court should have ensured the arrested person understood their rights and had a genuine opportunity to exercise them, especially when applying for interim release.

“The principal constitutional defect lay not in the absence of a fresh determination of probable cause–that question belonged to the issuing international court or tribunal—but in the total absence of any judicial review: former President Duterte was taken and flown to The Hague within hours, without any judicial imprimatur sought by his captors," Leonen said.
"That omission was a real violation of his right to be free from seizure except through judicial process,” he added.

Leonen acknowledged that surrendering Duterte and his former lieutenants has its advantages, but stressed that doing so does not represent complete accountability and should not stop the court from scrutinizing the process.

“Insisting on respect for human rights is not advancing a political cause or placing anyone beyond the reach of prosecution. It is insisting that justice be pursued through means worthy of its name-humane in application and legitimate in exercise,” Leonen said.

“A proper legal and just procedure for everyone matters. The procedure that protects a former president is the same procedure that protects the farmer taken at night and the young father picked up in an operation in a crowded barangay. Whatever we refuse to the powerful, we will soon be unable to guarantee to the powerless,” he added.
Dissenting opinions

The justices who voted against dismissing the petitions were Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando, retired Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier, Associate Justice Henri Jean Paul Inting and Associate Justice Antonio Kho Jr., according to the SC.

Hernando argued that Duterte’s surrender to the ICC violated constitutional rights including due process, protection against unreasonable searches and seizures, freedom of travel, and the rights of persons under custodial investigation.
He added that the former president’s surrender through Republic Act No. 9851 is unconstitutional.

Meanwhile, Lazaro-Javier rejected the majority’s view that the petitions had become moot, pointing out that the cases question the conduct of Philippine authorities rather than the ICC’s current custody of Duterte.
She explained that the legality of the respondent law enforcement officers’ acts—the arrest, detention, and rendition of Duterte to the ICC—is separate from the ICC’s custody.

She further stressed that a writ of habeas corpus examines not just physical detention, but also its legality and the constitutional principles involved, adding that the Executive branch’s decision not to seek Duterte’s repatriation remains open to judicial review.

For his part, Inting noted that determining whether the arrest and surrender followed the Philippine Constitution and domestic laws is a legal issue for the courts to resolve, not a political question left solely to the executive or legislative branches.

“The case continues to present a controversy on whether FPRRD was validly arrested and detained by the Philippine authorities on March 11, 2025, when he was surrendered to the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court (ICC). The issue is not a purely political question and should be resolved by the Court,” Inting said.

He also mentioned that an SC ruling could have practical value for ICC proceedings and case law, particularly under the abuse of process doctrine, where the ICC may suspend or terminate proceedings if improper or unlawful procedures were used to carry out an otherwise lawful process, such as an ICC arrest warrant.
'Sans domestic law, court authority'

Finally, Kho argued that the government cannot surrender a Filipino citizen to a foreign tribunal, or carry out an “extraordinary rendition,” without a valid domestic law and prior authority from the courts.
“Absent any such domestic law and prior judicial authorization, the extraordinary rendition of FPRRD to the ICC by the Philippine government is unconstitutional per se,” Kho said.

He also pointed out that if the SC were to dismiss the petitions as moot simply because Duterte had already been surrendered, similar actions in the future could evade judicial review just by being carried out quickly.

In March 2025, Duterte was transferred to the custody of the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands. He is set to stand trial for crimes against humanity before the ICC starting November 30, 2026. —NB, GMA News
